arXiv:2610.03902v1 [cs.CL] 02 Oct 2026

When Evidence Changes: Evaluating Memory Repair and Re-reading in Language-Model Agents

Wenhui Chu Affiliation: Department of Cybersecurity Affiliation: College of Emergency Preparedness, Homeland Security and Cybersecurity Affiliation: University at Albany, State University of New York Affiliation: Albany, NY 12222, USA Email: wchu3@albany.edu
Abstract

When documents supporting an agent’s derived facts are revoked or replaced, should it repair memory or re-read current evidence? We introduce an evidence-revision evaluation on medication- and problem-list tasks from public ICU records. Under revocation, replacement and control events, we compare full and source-filtered re-reading with caching, rebuilding and graph-local repair across two 7B models. Memory is supplied in full without retrieval, and costs include ingest, revision and every use. On short records, local repair uses 5–10×\times fewer revision tokens than rebuilding, yet every memory pipeline costs at least twice full re-reading in held-out conditions. In a small pre-specified development sweep, adding task-ineligible documents extended records to about 10,000 tokens; at that length, memory’s mean cumulative cost fell below full re-reading’s after 2–14 uses, partly through truncated extraction, while source-filtered re-reading remained cheapest. In the replacement study, none of the four primary confirmatory tests reached statistical significance. These results show why the cost of agent memory after evidence revision must be assessed against source-filtered re-reading over the full pipeline.

1 Introduction

A records assistant ingests a pharmacy record, extracts a medication, and writes a summary; later the connector revokes the record as misfiled. The raw record is marked revoked; the extracted claim and the summary are not, and in a new session the assistant builds a handoff list from memory. Nothing in this chain is an injection: the source was authentic when written and every write-time check passed. After a well-defined evidence revision, when should an agent maintain and repair derived memory, and when is re-reading the current evidence the better pipeline? We treat it as an evaluation question with three axes reported together: correctness under the revision, retention of still-valid information, and full pipeline cost, including initialisation, repair and every use.

Agent memory systems persist derived memory (Chhikara et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2026), and recent work shows that such memory can keep serving outdated or revoked facts (Chao et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026). Existing studies answer adjacent questions: repair systems score repair quality and operator cost against exhaustive repair (Zhao et al., 2026), maintained memory has been compared with full context on accuracy (Patel, 2026), and cost studies price memory against long context or full transcripts without revision-triggered repair (Pollertlam & Kornsuwannawit, 2026a; Pollertlam & Kornsuwannawit, 2026b) or, concurrently, meter memory operations and full-transcript replay (Mishra & Mishra, 2026). To our knowledge, none charges ingest, revision and every use against re-reading the current records, with and without source filtering, after a document is revoked or replaced (§2).

Under full-pipeline accounting, full re-reading was cheaper than every memory pipeline on the short records studied. Cost: graph-local repair’s revise phase cost 5–10×\times fewer tokens than rebuilding’s, yet its complete pipeline used 3.5–4.3×\times re-reading’s tokens on held-out patients, and reuse did not close the gap (§6.2). Length: when a pre-specified sweep lengthened the same records to about 10,000 tokens with chart documents the task does not use, the mean cumulative cost of all three memory pipelines fell below full re-reading’s after 2–14 uses, partly through truncated extraction; re-reading only the allowed sources stayed cheapest at every length, and even task-filtered memory used 1.4–1.5×\times as many tokens per use (§6.3). Replacement: re-reading adopted a replaced field for 13/13 development patients per model against 8–9/13 for rebuild and local repair, but every miss omitted a new value that was in the memory prompt, and most were lines already omitted before the revision; no 7B comparison of success (adoption with every other medication kept) between re-reading and these pipelines was significant, and none of the four primary tests of a pre-specified confirmatory replacement run (C2) rejected (§6.4). Revocation: no pipeline listed a revoked drug in 288 uses, as expected once the revoked document and derived nodes are removed, and a pre-specified held-out test at the small size did not detect an excess of non-allowed drugs under memory (§6.1).

This paper contributes (i) an evidence-revision protocol: allowed sources per task, a support class for every medication key, revocation, replacement and control events with expected answers, and endpoints for stale use, retention, adoption and cost (§3); (ii) full-pipeline accounting that charges ingest, revision and every use, with a standard break-even decomposition Δ​C​(k)\Delta C(k) and a source-filtered re-reading baseline, applied to memory pipelines that share extraction, a per-document versioned dependency graph and a read-set commit gate (§§4, 6.2); (iii) evidence from two open 7B models: development batches, a pre-specified held-out run, the confirmatory run C2 and a pre-specified length sweep, each labelled by evidential role in Table 16 (App. L); and (iv) a scorer-sensitivity audit of the problem-list task under lexical rules fixed after outputs were seen (§6.5).

Our threat model is narrow: an authentic connector revokes, replaces or adds documents; we model no adversary who writes documents, alters memory or injects instructions. Source permissions are stated in the use prompt and scored, not enforced (only two pipelines of §6.3 filter by source). The commit gate checks only that nothing an action read changed between snapshot and commit, not support, permission or freshness of rendered nodes (no-propagation committed superseded values), and never blocked a commit here. Zero counts are observations, not guarantees; record fidelity is not clinical validity; the ordering is a whole-pipeline result, not a mechanism attribution.

2 Related Work

Memory maintenance and repair in agents.

MemoRepair (Zhao et al., 2026) treats source deletion, correction and migration as repair events, withdraws the cascade reached through influence edges, and selects repaired successors to republish by a fixed-λ\lambda value–cost objective (min-cut); its value and cost terms are fixed inputs, and it gates only repaired successors, measuring downstream actions separately. Dependency-guided rollback repair (Yu et al., 2026) takes a failed trace and a diagnosed fault set, preserves nodes with independent support, and replays only answer-relevant steps; Infini Memory (Ji et al., 2026) consolidates memory into revisable topic documents and EvoMem (Xu et al., 2026) records patch-based update histories. He & Yu (2026) define typed provenance with supersession and revocation and mediate assertions at release, tested on 24 hand-authored cases without a language model. MemSecBench (Chen et al., 2026b) follows poisoned memory through a Write–Execute–Forget protocol with repair checkpoints. These works study how memory is maintained or repaired; we ask whether maintaining it is worth its full cost against re-reading.

Provenance, read-set validation and transactional commit.

MemLineage (Ouyang & Hou, 2026) signs entries, records a derivation DAG, verifies entries at retrieval and gates sensitive actions on lineage; TMA-NM (Louck, 2026) binds origin at write time with a machine-checked separation theorem. CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2026) and FIDES (Costa et al., 2025) enforce capability or information-flow policies at tool calls, evaluated on prompt injection in AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024). Their endpoints are attack success and task utility. EAL-Bench (Cerruti et al., 2026) shows that misrecorded permissions and revocations in memory can grant authority the history never permitted, without any attacker. Cordon (Chen et al., 2026c) validates a transaction over tool intents, lineage and staged effects before commit; MemTX (Li et al., 2026) stages memory writes in snapshot-isolated transactions, blocks irreversible tool calls while uncommitted beliefs are in flight and repairs derived records when a belief is retracted; MemTxn (Cui et al., 2026) admits an update only if its value is in the cited evidence and restores the application-visible state after faults; Khan (2026) formalises the stale-generation anomaly and verifies runtimes that prevent it; PlanFence (Chen et al., 2026a) has plans cite the records they used and, before an external action, validates only the records that can affect it, replanning or blocking when validation is incomplete. Our read-set commit gate is closest to these designs: it rejects commits whose read set changed and enforces no source-support, provenance, permission or information-flow policy.

Attacks, stale memory and record-level evaluation.

Memory poisoning is studied by AgentPoison (Chen et al., 2024, including an electronic-health-record agent), MPBench (Dash et al., 2026) and GhostWriter (Torres et al., 2026); these adversarial writes are outside our threat model. STALE (Chao et al., 2026) reports a gap between retrieving updated evidence and acting on it; Shen et al. (2026) find that no memory system of five enforces revocation in every case, over direct and extraction-based writes; the two that returned both the revoked record and its replacement (Graphiti by default, mem0 only with its default read-time filter overridden) ranked the revoked record first; StateAuditor (Sun & He, 2026) checks the provenance and chronology of state transitions before draft repair; TEPA (Zhou et al., 2026) makes validity a revocable state of evidence memory; and Supersede (Patel, 2026) measures update accuracy lost when bounded self-maintained memory replaces full context.

Cost of memory against long context and replay.

Pollertlam & Kornsuwannawit (2026a) price a Mem0-based fact memory (Chhikara et al., 2025), written once and read at a roughly fixed cost per turn, against long-context turns under prompt caching; memory became cheaper after about ten turns at 100k tokens, the direction of our length sweep at a tenth of that length. Their follow-up (2026b) meters three memory systems’ ingest, retrieval and answer calls against full-transcript resubmission (break-even from turn 0 to never within 400 turns); neither repairs memory nor filters re-reading by source. Concurrent work (MERIT; Mishra & Mishra 2026) meters every memory operation of tool-using agents, probes updated facts and finds full-transcript replay never the most cost-effective condition; our re-reading reads only current records and was cheaper than every memory pipeline on short ones. Wu & Canedo (2026) evict stale cached API-recovery suggestions by version stamp; row-level invalidation recovered 29–33 % of the token cost of a baseline that re-derives every episode, on four of seven models. Spencer (2026) finds full-history reading tied or beat memory at a short horizon, while at a long one a layered memory at about half the read cost was not reliably less accurate. AgingBench (Zhu et al., 2026) diagnoses four kinds of agent aging, including revision.

What this paper adds.

Cascade propagation, cost-aware repair, support preservation and commit-time validation are established mechanisms, and we claim no novelty for them (an adaptation of the MemoRepair selector is in Apps. K and M). We add the evidence-revision protocol, full-pipeline accounting against re-reading with and without source filtering, and the scorer-sensitivity audit.

3 Problem and Task Definition

Setting.

An agent serves a patient episode rendered as connector documents D1,…,DnD_{1},\dots,D_{n}, each with a connector-assigned source (pharmacy, ehr for electronic health record, lab), patient identifier, version and payload digest. A memory pipeline derives nodes (claims, i.e. extracted facts; per-document summaries; a global summary) from the documents; a re-reading pipeline derives nothing. A revision event changes one document version. Afterwards the agent answers use tasks; each answer is an action that a commit gate validates against the prompt’s snapshot.

Tasks and allowed sources.

Two use tasks follow every revision (the reuse and length sweeps of §§6.2 and 6.3 issue only the medication task): a handoff medication list, which may use only pharmacy documents, and an active problem list, which may use only the problem-list document. Only the currently active version of an allowed document supports an item; patient attribution is the connector’s field, never model text. Every pipeline’s use prompt states the allowed sources in the same words (a task contract hashed before any scenario existed).

Support classes.

For every medication key of the allowed documents’ MEDICATION lines the builder records its support set and a class: unique-support-revoked (must be absent after the revision), still supported (must remain), conflict (replacement), irrelevant (only non-allowed documents mention it; listing it is an unsupported-source error, not a stale error), or ambiguous (combination components, excluded from expected sets). The drug named by E4’s added record (below) is on no allowed line, so its key is added explicitly as irrelevant.

Revision events and controls.

E0: no revision. E1: a fourth authentic-source document carrying a real medication of a donor patient is revoked as misfiled after the first use. E1b: as E1, but the drug retains independent allowed support and must be retained. E4: no revision; a non-allowed treatment record naming an extra drug is added, and the answer must not change. E2: one pharmacy order is replaced by a second version in which exactly one explicit strength field is changed (a counterfactual 2×2\times change chosen by a pre-declared rule from lines that carry a strength; never a clinical claim); the new value must be adopted and every other valid medication retained.

Endpoints (over attempted trajectories; execution failures stay in the denominator).

Medication use: strict completion (listed generic-key set equals the expected set), stale commit (a unique-support-revoked key listed), unsupported-source and fabricated listings, missing keys, retention of the still-supported key. Replacement: new value adopted, old value retained, missing, other identities retained, success = adopted ∧\wedge other identities retained (identity level; an unsupported extra identity does not fail it—the stricter successstrict{}_{\text{strict}} that excludes it is reported for C2 and the 32B supplement, Apps. J and P). Problem list: the frozen leaf-match proxy, the record-fidelity rules of §6.5 and their relaxations, side by side. Cost: calls and prompt+completion tokens per phase.

Statistics.

The patient is the unit, except in batch E’s unit pairing (App. M) and one post-hoc pooled sign test (App. J); conditions, seeds and versions are never pooled. Within-patient comparisons use exact McNemar tests with Holm correction within each declared family (Holm-mm: a family of mm tests); the four C2 primary cells (two models ×\times two strata) are each tested alone at α=0.05\alpha=0.05, without correction across cells; hypotheses whose direction was fixed in advance (the held-out E4 and C2 primaries, the C2 adoption secondary and their 32B repeats) are one-sided, as is that sign test; all others are two-sided (Apps. C, J and P); proportions carry exact Clopper–Pearson 95 % intervals.

4 Pipelines

All memory pipelines (Fig. 1) share the extraction prompt, gateway, node representation and initial ingest; claims extracted from a document that changed before the write are rejected as stale input; validation and the action record form one transaction (App. A). The pipelines are: re-read (no memory; the current documents are placed in the prompt at use time), cache (per-document extraction cache; on revision re-extract the changed document only; no summary layer), rebuild (recompute every node after a revision), local repair (recompute only the invalidated nodes in dependency order: the changed document’s claims, its summary and the global summary), quarantine (invalidate the successors and recompute nothing), and no-propagation (called minimal authentication in the frozen plans: historical derived nodes stay eligible for rendering; a negative control, not a candidate design); the last two ran in the replacement batches only. The memory-pipeline use prompt shows all its summaries and facts (no retrieval) with claim identifiers and the parent document’s connector source; document versions are tracked by the host read set, not shown to the model. An adapted selector implements a published value–cost repair selector (App. K); it is an adaptation, not the published method, run once (§6.4).

5 Experimental Setup

Data.

Episodes come from the intensive care unit (ICU) records of the eICU Collaborative Research Database demo v2.0.1 (Pollard et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2021; Pollard et al., 2026), under a person-level split frozen before the experiments reported here (147 development / 54 calibration / 161 sealed people). “Held-out” means held out from protocol, prompt and scorer development: no agent output for a sealed patient existed before the held-out run, although the sealed records had been used in an earlier project split (disclosed in the pre-specification). The calibration partition was unused until the confirmatory replacement run of §6.4. Each episode is rendered as connector documents: medication orders, a problem list and laboratory results (small: 3 documents); the large size adds per-day order, laboratory and treatment documents (4–8 documents). Record payloads are short: 65–129 (small) and 210–558 (large) tokens for the eight development screening episodes and 59–155 for the 20 sealed held-out episodes (small only), counted as 1.3×1.3\times whitespace words; with document headers and tags, development small-size post-revision re-reading bodies are 251–373 Qwen2.5 tokens (App. O). The eICU medication table records orders, not confirmed administration (Pollard et al., 2018). Nothing is padded.

Models and decoding.

Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024) and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023; Mistral AI, 2025) ran on vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) at temperature 0 (seed 0) in every build stage. A labelled parser closes and logs Mistral’s truncated JSON (App. A).

Batches (Table 16, App. L).

Development screening and E1b/E4 controls (8 patients, both sizes); one held-out run (20 sealed patients, small size) submitted once and read once; replacement batch C (13 development patients), the shared-ingest batch E (the same 13 plus 4 screening patients) and the confirmatory C2; a same-facts ablation (batch A) and its decoding replay (batch B); a reuse sweep (EXP-R) and a length sweep (EXP-X). Every batch had its code, scenarios and the scoring contract of its pre-declared endpoints hashed before any model output of that batch existed, and every batch called pre-specified also had its analysis plan hashed in advance (“pre-specified” throughout means this prospective, in-project hash record; no external registry timestamp exists; Table 16 gives each batch’s role); the problem-list contract and its amendments (§6.5) are post-hoc instruments, fixed before re-scoring but after outputs had been seen.

6 Results

6.1 Revocation: stale commits, completion, retention and source compliance

Observed stale listings are zero in every cell where the endpoint applies. In the 288 post-revocation medication uses of the E1 screening and held-out runs (128 development: 8 patients ×\times 2 sizes ×\times 4 pipelines ×\times 2 models; 160 held-out: 20 ×\times 4 ×\times 2) no pipeline listed the unique-support-revoked key (E1b has no such key: its drug keeps independent support). Each E1 cell is 0 of 8 or 0 of 20 (exact 95 % interval for 0/200/20: 0–0.168); cells share patients, so no pooled bound is formed. Later E1 batches (batch E, the length sweep, the 32B runs) had none either. Every pipeline removes the revoked document or its derived nodes before the next use, so this endpoint verifies the implementation rather than separating pipelines; no positive control ran under revocation (no-propagation ran only under replacement, §6.4). Strict completion was low at the large size except for Mistral’s re-reading (Qwen 2–4 of 8; Mistral re-reading 7 of 8, memory 1–4) and mixed at the small size, mostly through missing orders; memory pipelines also listed drugs from non-allowed records (up to 3 of 8 in E1 cells, 4 in one E0 cell) and, for Mistral, names in no document (up to 3 of 8).

Retention and source compliance (development, 8 patients per cell). The still-supported drug was retained in 5–8 of 8 episodes in every E1b cell (App. C). Qwen’s re-reading listed no non-allowed drug in E4 at either size, while its memory pipelines did in 2–4 of 8 at both sizes; Mistral’s memory pipelines did in at most 1 of 8 at the small size, and rebuild and local repair in 6 and 5 of 8 at the large size (re-reading 1), where any drug from a non-allowed document counts. In each of the 10 small-size listings (Qwen cache 2, rebuild 3, local repair 4; Mistral local repair 1) the drug had entered memory as a medication fact whose parent is the non-allowed document, as it had in 38 trajectories that did not list it: the path shows how the drug reached the prompt, not why it was listed.

Pre-specified held-out run (20 sealed patients per model; Table 1). Its design, endpoint, test and stop rules were fixed before the agent protocol touched any sealed patient (App. C). The primary hypothesis—that the memory pipelines list a drug found only in a non-allowed document more often than re-reading—was not supported: Qwen 2, 0 and 1 of 20 (cache, rebuild, local repair) against 0 for re-reading (smallest one-sided p=0.25p=0.25); Mistral 1, 4 and 4 against 4, with balanced discordant pairs for rebuild and local repair (3/3 each) and 1/4 for the cache. The run used the small size only, where Mistral’s development listings had been rare (at most 1 of 8, against 5–6 at the large size). Later 32B analyses (App. P) are exploratory.

6.2 Cost: nodes recomputed versus tokens spent

Local repair does what it is designed to do: in all 32 E1 screening trajectories it invalidated exactly the three transitive successors of the revoked document and rebuilt one node, where rebuild recomputed 7–14.5 nodes, so its revise phase costs 5–10×\times less than rebuild’s (Fig. 3 and Table 5, App. D). But ingest and the memory-based use prompts dominate: in the E1 development cells the complete local-repair pipeline costs 3.96–5.03×\times the tokens of re-reading (rebuild 5.3–6.8×\times, cache 2.2–3.0×\times) because the extracted facts plus summaries are longer than the raw documents. The held-out run shows the same order: local-repair full-trajectory tokens were 3.5–4.3×\times re-reading’s over the four held-out conditions (Table 4, App. C; use-stage prompts alone 2.1–2.2×\times), and re-reading was cheapest in every held-out cell. At 32B the ordering is unchanged on the same eight patients: memory cost 2.3–6.5×\times re-reading’s tokens, with longer later uses in all six cells (App. P).

Why reuse does not rescue memory here.

For kk later uses the token difference between a memory pipeline and re-reading is Δ​C​(k)=Δ​I+Δ​U0+Δ​R+∑j=1k(Umem,j−Ureread,j)\Delta C(k)=\Delta I+\Delta U_{0}+\Delta R+\sum_{j=1}^{k}(U_{\mathrm{mem},j}-U_{\mathrm{reread},j}), where Δ​I\Delta I, Δ​U0\Delta U_{0} and Δ​R\Delta R are the ingest, initial-use (pre-revision) and revision differences, together the fixed difference, and U⋅,jU_{\cdot,j} is the token count of later use jj. Δ​I\Delta I and Δ​R\Delta R are non-negative by construction (re-reading performs no ingest and no revision work); Δ​U0\Delta U_{0} was non-negative in 11 of 12 cells of the 20-use sweep below. The per-use term decides whether reuse can ever pay. A pre-specified 20-use sweep on the eight development patients (128 trajectories, none failed; App. N) found it positive in 11 of the 12 model–size–pipeline cells (+175 to +2,276 tokens); local repair’s later uses cost 1.4–2.5×\times re-reading’s, and its cumulative ratio fell from 4.9–6.2×\times at k=1k=1 to 1.8–2.9×\times at k=20k=20 without reaching 1. The one exception, the Mistral large-size cache (−12.6-12.6 tokens per use against a fixed difference of 8,213; break-even near 652 uses, not observed), had shorter prompts, which in the screening run of that cell came from capped extractions that dropped laboratory content (App. E). No cell’s mean cumulative cost fell below re-reading’s by k=20k=20 (lowest ratio 1.21, 95 % interval 0.94–1.47): on these short records graph-local repair saves recomputation, not tokens.

6.3 Longer records: a pre-specified length sweep

A pre-specified development batch (EXP-X) stress-tested growth in content the task cannot use, with its plan, frozen code, scenarios and analysis program hashed before its first model call (App. O). On the eight development screening patients (E1, 20 later uses, both 7B models), each record was lengthened with the same patient’s laboratory, vital-sign and nursing-chart documents (whole documents per table and ICU day; nothing padded or synthesised), from sources the medication task does not allow, to four levels of the post-revision re-reading body: the small scenario (S) and targets of 1,000 (M), 4,000 (L) and 10,000 (XL) tokens (Qwen2.5 tokenizer; L is not the large size). A patient entered a level only if its re-reading body fell within 90–100 % of the target, giving 8, 3, 5 and 6 patients; each level is analysed on its own patients, and M is descriptive. Two source-filtered pipelines were added: re-reading that shows only allowed-source documents (RRTF), and task-filtered local repair (TF), which still ingests every added document but whose use prompt shows only allowed-source claims and those documents’ summaries. All 264 trajectories completed.

Results against the five pre-specified predictions (Fig. 2; App. O, Tables 20–26). At S the per-use difference was again positive for cache, rebuild and local repair in both models (P1). The per-use ratio to re-reading fell from S to XL in all six model–pipeline cells (P2, computed afterwards as the hashed program omitted it; Qwen 1.28–1.93 to 0.50–0.65, Mistral 1.34–2.03 to 0.14–0.23), though not monotonically for Qwen, whose ratios rose from S to M on the same three patients (local repair 1.86 to 2.08) before falling. At XL cache, rebuild and local repair all cost less per use than re-reading, with 95 % intervals excluding zero (P3), and cumulative cost crossed within 20 uses: at k=3k=3, 7 and 14 for Qwen’s cache, local repair and rebuild and at 2, 3 and 5 for Mistral’s; at L only Mistral’s three crossed (4, 8 and 15). These are crossings of the patient mean; the 95 % interval of the 20-use ratio still includes 1 for Qwen’s rebuild at XL and Mistral’s rebuild at L. Fed the fixed difference and uses 1–3, the identity predicted every observed crossing of a memory pipeline (15 cells, TF included) to within one use (P4), a weak test since per-use cost barely varied over 20 identical uses. Source-filtered re-reading was the cheapest pipeline at every level in both models (P5), at 0.70–0.72×\times re-reading’s 20-use tokens at S and 0.05×\times at XL, because it never pays for the added documents; TF’s per-use tokens remained 1.38–1.50×\times RRTF’s at every level. At L and XL, 225 of the 520 extraction calls on added documents stopped at the 2,048-token output cap (none of the 836 on the original documents at any level), and 44 Mistral extractions failed to parse even after repair, so part of memory’s per-use saving there is content that never entered memory; complete extractions would have added output and rendered claims, so these break-evens probably favour memory (not measured). P5 was largely implied by the design. Strict completion did not differ significantly from re-reading in any cell (Holm p=1.0p=1.0 throughout), and no trajectory listed the revoked key. Under the pre-specified cached-input pricing (input tokens that repeat the previous call’s prefix are billed at a fraction cc), we report Qwen only: the analysis program counted Mistral’s repeated prefixes with the Qwen2.5 tokenizer, so Mistral’s cached ratios are not valid and no claim uses them (its no-cache ratios come from server usage and are unaffected; App. O). At XL and k=20k=20, Qwen’s cache and local repair stayed below full re-reading at c=0.5c=0.5 (0.68, 0.92; rebuild 1.13), and none of the three did at c=0.1c=0.1 (1.13–2.37). Caching discounts the record that re-reading resends, not memory’s distinct extraction calls. Tokens were weighted equally; pricing output above input would raise memory’s fixed cost, since its extractions of added documents averaged about 1,500 output tokens each (App. O) while re-reading’s answers were short (98–118 completion tokens each, held-out run).

6.4 Replacement (batch C): adoption versus success

Thirteen development patients, each with one pharmacy order replaced by a counterfactual 2×2\times-strength version, were run through five pipelines and both models (130 trajectories; no execution failure; Table 14, App. I). Re-reading adopted the new value in 13/13 for both models; rebuild in 8/13 and 9/13; local repair in 9/13 and 8/13. No-propagation adopted it in 0/13 and listed the superseded value in 8/13 for both models; quarantine adopted it in 0/13 because invalidating without recomputing removes the line. On the success endpoint (adopted and every other medication identity retained) re-reading scored 9/13 and 10/13, below its adoption count, because it omitted other lines more often than rebuild and local repair (which kept them in 12/13 per cell). The batch’s pre-declared primary comparison (development evidence), local repair against re-reading on success, was 8 vs 9 (Qwen; discordant 2/3; p=1.0p=1.0) and 7 vs 10 (Mistral; 2/5; p=0.45p=0.45, Holm-2 p=0.91p=0.91): no detected difference at n=13n=13. Against the two controls (manipulation checks; neither adopted in any unit), local repair differed for Qwen (8 vs 0, Holm-6 p=0.047p=0.047) and not for Mistral (7 vs 0, Holm-6 p=0.0625p=0.0625). In all 18 rebuild and local-repair units that did not adopt, the new value was in the facts shown, so it had propagated and was left out of the answer; 16 of the 18 (five patients per model) had also left that line out before the revision, an association rather than an explanation (App. I, which also notes a spelling variant scored as missing plus unsupported).

Shared-ingest comparison and an adapted selector (batch E).

A pre-specified batch forked rebuild, local repair and the adapted value–cost selector of App. K (λ=0.3\lambda=0.3 and 1010) from one shared ingested state per unit (13 replacement and 8 revocation units, 17 patients; 210 trajectories, none failed; App. M). The adoption gap persisted: re-reading 13/13 for both models; rebuild and local repair 8–9/13 (Qwen) and 10/13 (Mistral). Between batches C and E (separate ingests, same 13 patients) memory adoption moved by 1–2 per cell, as much as memory pipelines differed.

Pre-specified replacement follow-up (C2).

Both models were evaluated on 8 calibration patients not previously used by the agent protocol (A) and 11 reused held-out patients (B), with five pipelines and a frozen scorer (190 trajectories, no failures). Re-reading adopted every replacement, but Mistral A success was 4/8 versus 6/8 for rebuild and local repair. None of the pre-specified primary paired adoption tests rejected the null (p=0.0625,0.5,0.0625,0.25p=0.0625,0.5,0.0625,0.25 for Qwen A, Mistral A, Qwen B and Mistral B); no secondary test survived Holm-3 (minimum adjusted p=0.1875p=0.1875). Figure 4 and Table 15 (App. J) give adoption and success separately. The runner made three use calls where the frozen plan specified two; adoption and success, scored on the second, are unaffected, and C2 cost is not used (App. J). An exploratory 32B repeat on reused records, run after the 7B results, rejected the C2 primary in two of three cells (per-cell α=0.05\alpha=0.05; one after Holm-3; App. P).

6.5 Problem-list scoring: post-hoc lexical sensitivity analysis

Instruments.

Both earlier scorers accepted wordings that a record-fidelity reading rejects, so we fixed a versioned record-fidelity contract (a path counts only when its entity and every recorded qualifier appear) and three amendments, each written after outputs had been seen (App. F).

Re-scoring (post hoc).

Table 6 (App. G) is a scorer-sensitivity analysis of E1 under seven lexical rules, not confirmatory evidence of record quality. Of 12 per-model memory-versus-re-reading comparisons (Holm-12), 0 to 12 were significant depending on the rule (Tables 7 and 8); re-reading was at or above the memory pipelines in every cell, but the counts are properties of the rule. Every rule is lexical; none is a pre-specified semantic endpoint or clinical adjudication.

Same-facts ablation (batch A) and decoding replay (batch B).

Batch A cloned one facts-and-summaries snapshot per patient, condition and model into four use branches (facts only, F; summaries then facts, SF; facts then summaries, FS; current documents, D). No patient-paired SF−-F difference in strict record fidelity was significant under any rule, and Mistral’s facts-only branch F still lay below D (8 vs 12 and 8 vs 11 of 16; Holm p=1.0p=1.0). Batch B re-issued the use calls at temperature 0.2 with two seeds: 1–2 of 128 fidelity-strict outcomes per model flipped and no primary cell was significant (App. H).

7 Discussion

What this comparison shows.

On short records local repair saved tokens against rebuilding but not against re-reading (§6.2). At about 10,000 tokens memory’s per-use term turned negative, but the saving came from replacing documents the task cannot use by short, partly truncated extractions, not from compressing the evidence it uses: task-filtered memory still cost 1.4–1.5×\times source-filtered re-reading per use. The baseline to beat is therefore the strongest re-reading pipeline (source filtering, cached input), not re-reading everything at full price. On correctness, re-reading’s 7B adoption lead held in direction in every C2 cell but reached α=0.05\alpha=0.05 in none, came without a significant lead on success, and in batches C and E every rebuild or repair miss left out a value its prompt contained, which locates the miss at use, not in propagation, but does not explain it.

Alternative explanations not excluded.

The extractor types every drug mention as a medication fact whatever its parent’s source (a treatment-record drug becomes med | … | from=D4:ehr), and problem-list facts appear as category-prefixed paths, so the E4 additions and the problem-list gap may be effects of extraction typing and presentation rather than of maintenance: hypotheses for an ablation, not findings.

8 Limitations

One dataset; two 7B models, with one later 32B exploratory supplement (App. P); greedy build stage; 3–20 development, calibration or sealed patients per cell, reused across pipelines and conditions. The length sweep reused the eight screening patients (3–8 per level, each level on its own patients), added only non-allowed documents, and weighted input and output tokens equally; its analysis program omitted one pre-specified prediction, and its cached-input sensitivity is valid for Qwen only (App. O). Scorers are lexical and were written after inspecting development outputs; no clinical adjudication exists; all contract and amendment numbers are post-hoc re-scorings of seen outputs. Replacement uses counterfactual strength changes only; there is no adversarial evaluation, one revision per trajectory, one repeated use template, and costs are tokens, not prices or latency. Greedy decoding was not bit-reproducible on the serving stack. Persistence, extraction/typing, summary, source rendering and prompts are not independently manipulated, so no causal maintenance effect is identified.

9 Conclusion

On short records re-reading had the lower full-pipeline token cost; with about 10,000 tokens of documents the task does not use, memory’s mean cumulative cost undercut full-record re-reading after 2–14 uses, partly through truncated extraction, but never source-filtered re-reading, which by design skipped those documents. Re-reading adopted replacements more often, without a significant 7B lead on success; neither confirmatory analysis (the held-out E4 primary tests and the four C2 primary tests) rejected, and since representations, prompts and persistence differ together, none of this shows that repair itself is ineffective. Progress still requires one pre-specified semantic endpoint, larger unseen samples, records that grow in allowed evidence and an information-matched compressive ablation.

AI use statement

Following the ICLR 2027 AI policy, each listed task is marked used, not used or not applicable. The language models evaluated in the experiments are the object of study and are not counted here. Required disclosures. Generate synthetic data sets: not used; evaluation scenarios, including the counterfactual revision events, are deterministic rule-based transformations of public de-identified records, produced by AI-assisted code. Help develop theoretical models or conceptual frameworks: used, to refine the evaluation framing and the cost-accounting decomposition. Formulate mathematical claims: used, to state and check the accounting identity Δ​C​(k)\Delta C(k) of §6.2. Provide critical ingredients for proving mathematical claims and assist in the writing of proofs: not applicable; the paper proves no theorem. Propose or refine hypotheses: used, including drafting the pre-specified predictions of the length sweep, which the author fixed before any model call. Design or provide feedback on research methodology or experiments: used. Implement methods: used, for the evaluation harness, scenario builder and analysis programs, which were checked against unit tests and pre-declared controls. Assist with translation: used. Clean and reformat dataset: used, through AI-assisted code that extracts and renders the eICU tables; no record content was edited by hand or by a model. Support qualitative and thematic data analysis: used only for model-assisted audits of outputs, treated as internal checks; every reported endpoint comes from a deterministic scorer. Interpret results: used. Recommended disclosures. Formulate questions for surveys or interviews, and transcribe recordings of research material: not applicable. Create or modify scientific figures or images, suggest experimental parameters, create or edit software code, and create artefacts: used. Draft parts of the paper, edit it for readability and suggest its structure: used; every statement was checked against the recorded results. Propose or refine the title or keywords: not used. Summarise or analyse existing literature, identify relevant literature, brainstorm, search for information, and format references: used; every reference was checked against its source. Discover research topics or identify gaps: not used. Reported values were recomputed from recorded outputs. The author reviewed all AI-assisted work and takes responsibility for the final text, claims, analyses, citations and artefacts.

Ethics statement

The records are de-identified, publicly released ICU data (eICU Collaborative Research Database demo v2.0.1, Open Data Commons Open Database License v1.0; no credentialing is required by the data provider); no new patient data were collected and no interaction with patients or clinicians took place, so no ethics approval was sought. All revision events are rule-based counterfactual edits of records, and every clinical-sounding output in this study is an evaluation artefact, not advice: we claim no clinical validity and no endpoint is a clinical adjudication. Any model outputs or scenario renderings shared during review or released later are derived from the demo data and released under its terms; the eICU event tables are not redistributed.

Reproducibility statement

Each batch used frozen code and scenarios and a scoring contract hashed before output, and recorded raw trajectories containing prompts, responses, usage, snapshots and read sets. These records reconstruct every held-out cell and its labels; re-scoring needs the scorer code. The length sweep’s plan, build, scenario manifest and analysis program were hashed before its first model call (App. O). The paper specifies the split, events, pipelines, models, decoding, endpoints and tests. A fresh model run needs the code, public weights, vLLM, a GPU and the open-access eICU demo tables, which we do not redistribute. No code or data accompany this preprint. Code will be released upon acceptance, together with the archive described in App. B (scenarios, raw trajectories, per-example outcomes and generated tables).

Appendix A Harness details and tested properties

Store.

Evidence rows carry (id, version, source, patient, payload digest, status); node rows carry (id, version, type, content digest, parents with the parent versions seen, status, creating session, snapshot id). A snapshot is one read transaction over active evidence and active nodes; its identifier is a content hash. Claims are admitted through a gateway (authorised source, i.e. a connector source the harness may ingest, distinct from a task’s allowed sources; same patient namespace; active evidence) inside one immediate transaction that rejects the whole batch as stale input if any shown evidence changed version. The commit gate validates every evidence version and every node’s own parent versions from the snapshot read set inside one transaction with the action record. It ensures only that no row in this read set changed between the snapshot and the commit; it does not check support, source permission, factual correctness or whether a rendered node reflects the latest document version (under no-propagation, nodes derived from a superseded version stay renderable and their actions commit), and it never blocked a commit in the sequential runs reported here.

Six deterministic properties (scripted clients, no model).

H1 revision after snapshot blocks the commit; H2 an unrelated write does not; H3 stale-input rejection of extraction; H4 exact transitive-successor invalidation; H5 dependency-ordered local rebuild; H6 read-set constraints are per node, never flattened. A seventh scripted case demonstrates a limit: unsupported content emitted by an extractor carries its chunk’s parent and survives another document’s revocation.

Prompts.

Extraction: one document per call, the document shown with its connector source, patient and version tag, returning candidate facts with an evidence reference; references outside the shown document are gated out. Summaries: per document from the admitted facts, then a global summary from these per-document (chunk) summaries. Use: the memory pipelines show the summaries and the facts as - <type> | <content> | claim=<id> | from=<document>:<source>; the version of each document is tracked by the host read set and is not shown to the model. Re-reading shows the current documents with their source and version tags. The allowed-source sentence is identical across pipelines; the task sentence differs only by the phrase “from these documents” appended for re-reading; all pipelines share one system prompt, which was written for the memory setting (“You have persistent memory about ONE patient from earlier sessions, shown below”) and is therefore not a perfect description of the re-reading prompt. Every extracted drug mention is typed as a medication fact whatever its parent’s connector source, so a drug named in a treatment record appears in the memory prompt as a medication fact tagged from=D4:ehr.

Parse repair.

Of the extraction calls of the screening jobs, most parsed strictly; Mistral’s outputs frequently lacked a closing brace and were repaired by a labelled deterministic parser that never alters a kept field; length-capped outputs keep only a complete prefix, so parseable is not complete. Every repair is recorded per call. In the replacement batch Mistral used the repair on 130 of 273 extractions and Qwen on 0.

Appendix B Artefact availability and event-level audit trail

The evidence archive is a hash-addressed archive with a manifest and checksum ledger. It packages the frozen E1/E1b/E2/E4 scenario inputs (pseudonymous patient identifiers, rendered evidence documents, active versions, revision event, target support class and expected endpoint), the raw run directories (prompts, responses, per-call usage, snapshots, read sets, parent versions, commit records and run status), the outcome labels and scorer explanations, and the pre-specification files and amendments; it does not contain source code. Any copy provided to reviewers passes identifying strings through a consistent anonymisation map, and its ledger is authoritative for that copy. Neither the archive nor the code is public at the time of this preprint; both will be released upon acceptance (App. L).

With our audit scripts (not in the archive), from these raw records the reported held-out medication cells and E4 primary tests are re-derived, the raw model text re-scored, E4 prompt provenance verified, the C2 scorer checked against destructive corruptions, and the reuse and 32B summaries regenerated; the frozen scenario files are sufficient to audit the revision labels and denominators. Without source code, this supports reconstruction of the reported results from the raw records but not a fresh model run, which also needs public weights, vLLM, a GPU and the open-access eICU demo tables (not redistributed). The event-level records, raw trajectories and outcome labels are the auditable evidence.

Appendix E Representation ratio

The task-scoped representation ratio ρtask\rho_{\text{task}} has a median above one in all 30 groups of the current screening runs (smallest 1.23). This is a CPU-filtered block ratio, not a task-filtered model run. The unscoped ratio ρall\rho_{\text{all}} falls below one in two Mistral large-cache groups (0.93 and 0.94), with extraction truncation and missing laboratory content. Neither ratio is the full per-use token cost (§6.2).

Two ratios are defined for a memory-pipeline use prompt and the re-reading prompt of the same scenario and use index, both counted with the model’s own tokenizer on the prompt bodies (instruction text excluded): ρall\rho_{\text{all}} = memory-block tokens / tokens of all active document bodies shown to re-reading; ρtask\rho_{\text{task}} = tokens of the task-filtered memory block (medication facts and summaries of pharmacy documents for the medication task; problem-list facts and summary for the problem-list task) / tokens of the task-allowed document bodies. The task filter is a CPU reconstruction of the recorded blocks. Two measurements exist and are reported separately. (i) An earlier measurement (eight development patients; 144 pairs per job; 18 groups = job ×\times task ×\times memory pipeline): group medians ≥1\geq 1 for both ratios (smallest 1.20 for ρall\rho_{\text{all}}, 1.01 for ρtask\rho_{\text{task}}); pairs below one: 6 of 432 (ρall\rho_{\text{all}}) and 69 of 432 (ρtask\rho_{\text{task}}). (ii) The screening batches of this paper (768 recorded use prompts, 576 pairs, 30 groups; tokenised in a CPU job whose chat-template token counts equal the served prompt tokens for 768 of 768 prompts): ρtask\rho_{\text{task}} medians ≥1\geq 1 in all 30 groups (smallest 1.23; 6 of 576 pairs below one); ρall\rho_{\text{all}} medians ≥1\geq 1 in 28 groups, below one in the two Mistral large-size cache groups (0.93 and 0.94; 24 of 576 pairs below one, all in these groups), where 11 of the 116 cache extraction calls ended at the 2,048-token cap and the memory therefore lacks laboratory content—an incompleteness effect, not a compressive representation. Neither measurement supports a group-level compression advantage for maintained memory; the run directories of (i) are not in the App. B archive (their token counts are), those of (ii) are.

Appendix F Problem-list scoring contract

Instruments and their defects.

The screening runs scored the problem list with a leaf-match proxy (a truth path’s last segment matched by an item), which accepts “no chest pain” and “chest pain and sepsis” for “chest pain”. A record-fidelity scorer separated parent-only, bundled, negated and uncertain items, but a last-segment-only item (“acute”) passed its strict rule without naming the disease, a verbatim echo of a full path could be labelled bundled when sibling paths share a parent, and punctuation was removed before the bundle check; such a rule can itself create discordant pairs between pipelines.

Truth structure.

A path s1​|s2|​c1​|…|​cks_{1}|s_{2}|c_{1}|\dots|c_{k} has a category (s1,s2s_{1},s_{2}; never sufficient) and a concept chain; the disease entity EE is the first chain segment that is not a qualifier (severity, laterality, cause, status such as “s/p”, “acute”, “with …”, ranges); later chain segments are qualifiers, and every chain segment is task-required because the record states it.

Coverage and outcomes.

An item covers a path fully when it equals the path or its chain, or contains every chain segment as a whole phrase in any order (“acute hepatic dysfunction” covers hepatic dysfunction|acute); it covers the entity when EE is present but a qualifier is missing (partial_parent, with a qualifier_lost flag); it is qualifier_only when only qualifiers are present. A full cover of one path is never a parent hit of a sibling path. Bundling is decided on fragments split at “,” “;” “&” “and” before normalisation; a fragment inside the assigned path’s own text is never an extra. Placeholders (<…>, “…”, “diagnosis value”) are uncertain. Leading negation or status cues are retained when they are part of the covered path (“s/p CABG”) and otherwise make the item negated. Outcome precedence: uncertain, negated, extra_bundled, exact, partial_parent, qualifier_only, unmatched.

Endpoints.

strict: format valid, committed, every path covered exactly, no other item. Relaxations recorded separately: LparentL_{\text{parent}} (partial_parent covers), LextraL_{\text{extra}} (unmatched items allowed), LbundleL_{\text{bundle}} (bundled covers); lenient = all three; qualifier_only, negated and uncertain items never pass. Format failures, blocked and empty outputs are attempted, never success.

Summary and effect of the amendments.

Three amendments followed, each written after outputs had been seen and disclosed as such: amendment 1 (wording artefacts of our own rule), amendment 2 (exact-match priority for nested chains; postposed cues; parenthetical abbreviations only when traceable), and amendment 3 (cue scope per occurrence; constrained abbreviation matching), the last closing two synthetic false acceptances found by later reviews. Under amendment 2 a verbatim echo of all 36 real truth lists passes (34 under amendment 1, 28 under fidelity); the amendment-2 defects changed no trajectory endpoint and one real item label (a batch-A “DKA (Diabetic Ketoacidosis)” item); amendment 3 changes 0 endpoints and 0 item labels of the 1,618 recorded outputs.

Amendment 1.

Written after the contract re-scoring was read (disclosed): connectives are all function words; words of the path’s recorded category are not extras; a parenthetical restatement or abbreviation of the covered path is not an extra; seven added controls (control set C15 of the scorer’s test suite).

Amendment 2.

Written after the final independent audit (disclosed): an item equal to a full path or its chain is assigned to that path only, and nested chains are resolved by specificity (the more specific covered path wins when the item’s content words lie within it); cue words are never connectives, and a postposed or mid-item cue (“pneumonia ruled out”, “pneumonia; resolved”) makes the item negated unless the cue is part of a covered path segment; a parenthetical abbreviation is permitted only when traceable to the assigned path (initials of its words, or the token occurs in the path text), otherwise it is content and the item is bundled; capitalisation never grants permission; no external dictionary or model is used. Control sets C16–C19 include verbatim echoes of all 36 distinct real truth lists and the audit’s ten adversarial cases. Results under every rule variant are reported.

Amendment 3.

Written after two later reviews (disclosed; post hoc like the earlier amendments): (a) a cue occurrence is retained only while the covered path segments contain at least as many occurrences of that cue phrase, so a second “without” that denies the entity makes the item negated while the recorded “without hemodynamic compromise” qualifier keeps its one occurrence; (b) a parenthesised token is a permitted abbreviation only if it occurs in the assigned path’s text or its letters are word initials of the path’s chain or category words in order, with at most one letter matched inside the previous word and only for tokens of three or more letters (COPD, CAD, DKA pass; PE and PUMA for “pneumonia” are extras). Ten added controls (control set C20); 111 controls pass; the re-scoring of all 1,618 recorded outputs changes 0 endpoints and 0 item labels. A three-letter token with two initials and one in-word letter (“CAT” for “coronary artery disease”) is still accepted and recorded as a known residual of the lexical rule.

Controls.

Fourteen control families with success counterparts for every failure case (full-path echo of every truth list, chain-only echo, natural-order phrase, qualifier-only, entity without qualifier, four punctuation bundles, a legitimate comma, placeholders, documented status, negation, an extra disease, execution states, sibling paths, and the 16 batch-A truth lists: full-path echo must pass 16/16 and last-segment-only echo must fail wherever a qualifier leaf exists). The implementation was hashed after the controls passed and before any real output was re-scored.

fidelity →\to contract: full-path echoes no longer labelled bundled (held-out / A / B: 49 / 25 / 50 outputs fail→\topass); last-segment-only items no longer passing (10 / 4 / 9 pass→\tofail; one qualifier-only, the rest deeper-concept-only such as “lactic acidosis” for “metabolic acidosis||lactic acidosis”); wording extras under the contract’s literal fragment rule (3 / 8 / 16 pass→\tofail); one further held-out partial-item flip (pass→\tofail); punctuation bundles, placeholders and status cues: no real output. contract →\to amendment 1: 42 outputs change an item label (function words, restated categories, article inside a qualifier); strict flips: held-out 0, batch A 5 fail→\topass, batch B 8 fail→\topass, none pass→\tofail; wording additions outside the recorded text (“…including …”, “such as”) remain extras by the literal rule and account for the residual batch-A/B failures they cause (5 and 12). Appendix H Batch A and batch B details

Batch A design.

One facts-and-summaries snapshot per patient, condition and model, built once with the real ingest path and cloned read-only into four use branches; the facts are byte-identical across F, SF and FS and the summaries across SF and FS (asserted at run time from recorded hashes). Each branch answers both tasks under E0 and E4 with one decoding on 16 development patients chosen by a pre-fixed eligibility rule and seed. The D branch shows the current documents with source and version tags; the memory branches show claim identifiers and connector sources, and versions are host-tracked. Integrity: 512 of 512 use outputs, 64 of 64 units passing the invariants, no format failure, blocked or empty output. No padding controlled the prompt-length difference between F and SF.

Counts behind §6.5.

On the patient-paired SF−-F difference in strict record fidelity (four cells, one Holm family; Tables 9 and 10) no cell is significant under any rule, but the counts move with it: under fidelity strict, Qwen E0 11 vs 11 of 16, E4 10 vs 11, Mistral E0 6 vs 8, E4 7 vs 8 (Holm p=1.0p=1.0 each); under amendment 2 strict, Qwen 13 vs 13 and 11 vs 13, Mistral 4 vs 10 (discordant 0/6; Holm p=0.125p=0.125) and 4 vs 10 (1/7; p=0.211p=0.211) of 16 (Table 11). For Mistral the documents branch scored 12 and 11 of 16 (fidelity) and F lay below D under every rule, so the gap is present without the summary; whether the summary lowers fidelity further depends on how wording additions (“…including …”) are scored—they remain extras under amendment 2 and account for the residual SF failures—and we do not claim it.

Batch B.

The use calls were re-issued at temperature 0.2 with two seeds: 17/256 (Qwen) and 36/256 (Mistral) raw outputs changed between seeds, 1–2 of 128 fidelity-strict outcomes per model flipped against seed 0, and no primary cell is significant under fidelity (Holm p=1.0p=1.0; Table 12) or amendment 2 (smallest Holm-8 p=0.562p=0.562; Table 13).

Appendix I Replacement batch: eligibility and per-configuration counts

Eligibility was decided from the input record by the frozen field-level scorer before any model output: a medication line with exactly one explicit strength field and no unsupported numeric expression, whose drug identity is unique and unambiguous among the allowed lines; the new value replaces the strength number by 2×2\times (else 0.5×0.5\times; all 13 pairs are 2×2\times). Of 27 development patients considered, 13 carried an eligible line (16 requested; not padded); the 13 targets cover seven distinct line texts and six drug identities. Outcome distribution: no-propagation 8 old-retained and 5 missing per model; quarantine 13 missing; re-read 13 adopted; rebuild 8/9 adopted and 5/4 missing; local repair 9/8 adopted and 4/5 missing (Qwen/Mistral). No unit listed both versions of the target; no unit’s target field was labelled an unsupported addition. Mean calls and tokens per trajectory: re-read 3 and 1.9k–2.2k; no-propagation and quarantine 12 and 6.3k–8.4k; local repair 15 and 7.8k–9.6k; rebuild 21 and 10.1k–12.5k.

Two readings that need care.

First, target-field labels say nothing about other fields; one Mistral patient’s enoxaparin line was spelled “ENOKAPARIN” in all five pipelines, which the lexical rule counts as a missing plus an unsupported identity. Second, in all 18 rebuild/local-repair units that did not adopt the new value (9 per model), the new text was in the facts shown, and most of these units had also left that line out before the revision (Qwen 9 of 9, Mistral 7 of 9)—an association on five patients per model, not a causal attribution.

Secondary family (Holm-6).

Local repair against no-propagation, quarantine and rebuild on success for both models, in one family of six two-sided exact McNemar tests (the first two are controls that adopted in no unit). Qwen: local repair vs no-propagation 8 vs 0 (Holm-6 p=0.0469p=0.0469); Qwen: local repair vs quarantine 8 vs 0 (Holm-6 p=0.0469p=0.0469); Qwen: local repair vs rebuild 8 vs 7 (discordant 1/0, Holm-6 p=1.0p=1.0); Mistral: local repair vs no-propagation 7 vs 0 (Holm-6 p=0.0625p=0.0625); Mistral: local repair vs quarantine 7 vs 0 (Holm-6 p=0.0625p=0.0625); Mistral: local repair vs rebuild 7 vs 8 (discordant 0/1, Holm-6 p=1.0p=1.0) (the family behind the §6.4 values).

Appendix J Confirmatory replacement run (batch C2): pre-specification and results

Pre-specification.

The plan (hashed before any scenario was generated; amendment hashed before any model output) fixed: the same five batch-C pipelines and both models with identical snapshots and decoding (temperature 0, seed 0); a frozen build (the batch-C build plus partition and stage selection options), hash-listed before submission; the frozen field-level scorer; the patient as unit; primary hypothesis (labelled Q1 in the frozen plan), one-sided exact McNemar at α=0.05\alpha=0.05: re-reading adopts the new value more often than local repair; secondary family (Holm-3 per model and stratum): re-reading versus rebuild on adoption (one-sided), and local repair and rebuild versus re-reading on success (two-sided); exact Clopper–Pearson intervals; no pooling across strata or models; the result is reported whatever its direction. Plan amendment (before any output). The plan intended the never-used sealed patients; the eligibility pass showed that all 20 generic-eligible sealed patients had been consumed by the held-out run, so the run was split into stratum A: all 8 E2-eligible patients of the calibration partition (54 people; never used by any model run of this project, checked against every run directory; record-level exposure by the earlier project split of §5 is not excluded), and stratum B: the 11 E2-eligible held-out patients (second use of those records; disclosed as such). Eligibility was decided from the input record by the frozen rule of App. I (all pairs 2×2\times). With n=8n=8 the one-sided test at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 rejects only when five or more discordant pairs all favour re-reading (5:0 to 8:0), or when all eight pairs are discordant and split 7:1; stratum A therefore has power only against a large effect and its interval, not its pp-value, is the informative summary.

Execution.

One job per model (two GPU-hours reserved; one 80–96 GB data-centre GPU each), stratum A then B on one served model, 40 and 55 trajectories per model; run status, code hash and scenario hash are recorded in the run directory and checked by the scoring script against the frozen list before scoring.

Post-run protocol erratum (2026-09-18).

The frozen C2 plan describes two use calls and says that problem-list use is excluded. The frozen runner and all 190 recorded trajectories instead execute three calls: medication before revision, medication after revision, and a later problem-list use. Adoption and success are scored on the second call, so their definitions and reported counts are unchanged. Full-trajectory cost includes the additional call. This is a protocol–execution discrepancy, not an amendment made before the run; the original plan and hashes are retained.

Post-hoc pooled sign test.

Post hoc; contrary to the pre-specified no-pooling rule; reported for completeness only. Pooling the two strata within a model (patients are never pooled across models, which share them) gives 8 of 8 discordant pairs favouring re-reading for Qwen (one-sided sign test p=0.0039p=0.0039) and 3 of 3 for Mistral (p=0.125p=0.125). The 11 pairs are 11 patient–model units, not 11 independent patients, and this is not a confirmatory result: the four pre-specified primary cells above are the confirmatory analysis and none rejected.

Appendix K Adapted published repair selector

We implemented a paper-based adaptation of the barrier-first cascade repair of Zhao et al. (2026) as a configuration of our harness (adapted selector). As of September 2026 we found no author-released implementation (arXiv abstract and full text, and a public code search); this does not establish that none exists. The adaptation keeps the published structure: influence edges are our host-recorded parents; the cascade C⁡(F)C(F) is the invalidated root set FF (here the revised document) and its transitive successors; every member of C⁡(F)C(F) is withdrawn (barrier) before any operator runs; a deterministic mode map assigns recompute to the claims of a corrected document, remove to the claims of a revoked one and regen to summaries with retained support; executability is checked; the selection maximises ∑iwi​xi−λ​∑ici​xi\sum_{i}w_{i}x_{i}-\lambda\sum_{i}c_{i}x_{i} under predecessor closure, where ii ranges over the non-removed descendants, xi∈{0,1}x_{i}\in\{0,1\} marks a selected candidate, wiw_{i} and cic_{i} are its value and cost (our proxies are given below) and λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 is the trade-off weight (solved exactly by enumeration on our small cascades, where the paper uses a min-cut); unselected members stay withdrawn; a recomputed or regenerated node is republished only after a schema check and (our addition) a truth-free provenance check (its inputs are still active at the shown versions); leak, republication rate and normalised operator cost are recorded per revision. Deviations, stated rather than emulated: semantic (retrieval) edges do not exist here and are not needed by the cascade; the migrate event and the param mode have no counterpart; the paper assigns modes by artefact class (recompute for replayable deterministic artefacts), and we treat temperature-0 claim extraction as replayable; claims of a revoked document are assigned remove, whereas the paper treats deterministic descendants of a deleted source as structurally non-executable candidates, which enter its republication-rate denominator; our operator costs are prompt characters over a predicted full-rebuild baseline, a prompt-length proxy, not tokens or the paper’s Repair-all cost, so λ=0.3\lambda=0.3 matches the paper’s value only numerically; the published paper defines the value wiw_{i} and cost cic_{i} only as fixed value–cost terms, so ours are observable proxies (pre-event dependents +1+1; predicted prompt characters); the paper’s task-regression and replay-consistency validators have no counterpart, and no experiment gold is read at repair time. Deterministic tests (scripted clients, development scenarios): independent support survives an unrelated revocation (19 untouched nodes keep version and digest); the barrier equals the transitive reach; on the replacement graph the selected set is {c⁡(D4),s⁡(D4),G}\{c(\mathrm{D4}),s(\mathrm{D4}),G\} (node names as in Fig. 1) for λ∈{0,0.3,1}\lambda\in\{0,0.3,1\}, {c⁡(D4),s⁡(D4)}\{c(\mathrm{D4}),s(\mathrm{D4})\} at λ=10\lambda=10, {c⁡(D4)}\{c(\mathrm{D4})\} at 30 and ∅\emptyset at 100; a no-revision scenario triggers no operator. On these chain-shaped cascades the λ=0.3\lambda=0.3 of the paper’s main configuration selects the same operator set as local repair (3 calls), so the two configurations differ only when validation fails (a malformed regenerated summary stays withdrawn under the adapted selector and is republished as raw text by local repair) or when λ\lambda exceeds the per-node thresholds. Whether this changes real-model outcomes was tested in a pre-specified development batch whose results are reported in App. M.

Appendix L Batches and cost

Each model-run batch used a frozen, hash-listed code build; builds advanced monotonically as options were added (partition and stage selection for the confirmatory replacement run; a repeated-use option and a model-registry entry for the reuse sweep and 32B supplement; length levels and two source-filtered use renderings for the length sweep), with no change to any scorer between them. The length-sweep plan records the Hugging Face snapshots of the two 7B tokenizers (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct revision a09a354, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 revision c170c70) and states that every batch served the models at the same snapshot revisions. Jiang et al. (2023) describe the original Mistral 7B release and are cited for the model family; the v0.3 checkpoint is described in its Hugging Face model card (Mistral AI, 2025). The problem-list scoring contract and its three amendments are post-hoc instruments, each hashed before the re-scoring it was applied to. Every batch had its scenarios, run configuration and the scoring contract of its pre-declared endpoints hashed before submission, and every job’s completion state was recorded. Total GPU time of the 61 GPU jobs that consumed time is 73,137 GPU-seconds (20.32 GPU-hours; one 80–96 GB data-centre GPU per job): 37,566 through C2 (pilots, smoke tests and cancelled jobs included), 337 for the 32B serving check, 5,014 for the reuse sweep, 3,140 for the 32B E1 supplement, 4,929 for the 32B replacement supplement, 813 for four 32B revocation launches that failed before producing output, 8,853 for the 32B revocation supplement, and 12,485 for the length sweep (11,629 batch, 382 serving check, 474 pilot). The batches listed in Table 16 account for 55,182 of these GPU-seconds; the remaining 17,955 are the serving checks and the pilots, smoke tests and cancelled jobs that produced no reported result. Site charges are unverified. Code will be released upon acceptance; on release the archive will contain the code, frozen inputs, raw trajectories, scoring outputs, re-scoring diffs and audit scripts. Any anonymous evidence provided during review is a redacted derivative: text passed through a fixed identity map, run directories with user, account, host and home-path strings replaced by placeholders, and trajectory and result files unchanged.

Appendix M Batch E: adapted selector from one shared ingest

Both runs completed (105 of 105 trajectories per model, 0 failed). Per model, 21 units (17 distinct development patients: 13 replacement units and 8 revocation units) were run through five pipelines; the four memory pipelines were forked from one shared ingested state per unit (byte-copied store; its hash is recorded in every row).
